claim: Chat i-Cre; Rosa26 lsl-ChR2-EYFP mice expressed ChR2-EYFP throughout the forebrain, recapitulating known patterns of Chat expression in cortex (Ctx), striatum, globus pallidus externus (GP), and nucleus basalis (NB).
source: Chat i-Cre; Rosa26 lsl-ChR2-EYFP mice expressed ChR2-EYFP throughout the forebrain, recapitulating known patterns of Chat expression in cortex (Ctx), striatum, globus pallidus externus (GP), and nucleus basalis (NB, Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing ChR2-EYFP expression pattern in mouse forebrain sections, and by established knowledge of Chat expression patterns.

claim: ChR2+ neurons in cortex and nucleus basalis are immunopositive for ChAT.
source: In both regions, ChR2+ neurons were immunopositive for ChAT, confirming our ability to selectively activate endogenous Chat+ inputs to cortex.
evidence: Supported by ChAT immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Layer 1 is strongly innervated by ChAT+ cells of the basal forebrain across species.
source: Layer 1 is strongly innervated by ChAT+ cells of the basal forebrain across species (Mesulam, 1995; Mechawar et al., 2000) including in Chat i-Cre; Rosa26 lsl-ChR2-EYFP mice, where ChR2-EYFP is expressed in a dense plexus (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and by imaging data in Figure 1C,D showing dense ChR2-EYFP expression in layer 1.

claim: In a subset of layer 1 interneurons (n = 41 of 58 cells from 9 mice), robust excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) were observed at −70 mV in response to brief pulses of blue light.
source: As expected, in a subset of interneurons (n = 41 of 58 cells from 9 mice), we observed robust excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at −70 mV in response to brief pulses of blue light (2–7 ms, Figure 1E, left).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs in layer 1 interneurons were not blocked by NBQX and CPP, ruling out a glutamatergic source.
source: These EPSCs were not blocked by NBQX and CPP, ruling out a glutamatergic source, but were blocked by the nicotinic ACh receptor (nAChR) antagonists DHβE, MLA, and MEC, confirming their cholinergic identity (nEPSCs).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing EPSCs persist in presence of glutamate receptor antagonists but are blocked by nAChR antagonists.

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs in layer 1 interneurons were blocked by the nicotinic ACh receptor (nAChR) antagonists DHβE, MLA, and MEC, confirming their cholinergic identity.
source: These EPSCs were not blocked by NBQX and CPP, ruling out a glutamatergic source, but were blocked by the nicotinic ACh receptor (nAChR) antagonists DHβE, MLA, and MEC, confirming their cholinergic identity (nEPSCs).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments demonstrating blockade by nAChR antagonists.

claim: nEPSCs displayed a typical biphasic response, with a fast component likely mediated by synaptic receptors containing the low-affinity α7 nAChR subunit, and a slow component likely mediated by non-synaptic receptors expressing the high-affinity non-α7 subunits.
source: nEPSCs displayed a typical biphasic response, with a fast component, likely mediated by synaptic receptors containing the low-affinity α7 nAChR subunit, and a slow component, likely mediated by non-synaptic receptors expressing the high-affinity non-α7 subunits (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by observed biphasic kinetics in recordings and cited literature on nAChR subtypes.

claim: Barrages of outward inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) were observed at 0 mV in layer 1 interneurons (n = 28 of 58 cells), indicative of signaling through GABA receptors.
source: In addition to the expected nEPSCs recorded at −70 mV, we also observed barrages of outward inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at 0 mV, indicative of signaling through GABA receptors (n = 28 of 58 cells, Figure 1E, center).
evidence: Supported by voltage-clamp recordings at 0 mV showing outward currents characteristic of GABA receptor activation.

claim: In a subset of recorded cells, IPSCs remained after application of nAChR antagonists (n = 9 of 58 cells), suggesting these PSCs were not dependent on nAChR signaling.
source: However, in a subset of recorded cells IPSCs remained (n = 9 of 58 cells, Figure 1F, right), suggesting that these PSCs were not dependent on nAChR signaling.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing persistence of IPSCs after nAChR blockade.

claim: Bath application of TTX blocked light-evoked nAChR-resistant IPSCs.
source: To test if nAChR-resistant IPSCs are caused by direct release of GABA from cholinergic fibers, we bath applied the voltage-gated sodium channel antagonist TTX, which blocked light-evoked IPSCs (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1F,G demonstrating TTX blockade of IPSCs.

claim: In the presence of TTX, IPSCs could be rescued by enhancing ChR2-mediated depolarization with the voltage-gated potassium channel blocker 4AP.
source: In the presence of TTX, IPSCs could be rescued by enhancing ChR2-mediated depolarization with the voltage-gated potassium channel blocker 4AP.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing recovery of IPSCs with 4AP application after TTX blockade.

claim: Rescued IPSCs in the presence of TTX and 4AP were blocked by the GABAA receptor antagonist SR95531 (n = 5 cells from 4 mice).
source: Rescued IPSCs were subsequently blocked by the GABAA receptor antagonist SR95531 (n = 5 cells from 4 mice).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments demonstrating SR95531 blockade of rescued IPSCs.

claim: nAChR-resistant 'direct' IPSCs had faster average onsets (2.5 ± 0.2 ms, n = 9 cells) than both nEPSCs (4.0 ± 0.2 ms, n = 41 cells) and nAChR-sensitive 'indirect' IPSCs (11.8 ± 2.3 ms, n = 19 cells from 9 mice).
source: Moreover, nAChR-resistant 'direct' IPSCs had faster average onsets than both nEPSCs and nAChR-sensitive 'indirect' IPSCs (nEPSCs, 4.0 ± 0.2 ms, n = 41 cells; direct IPSCs, 2.5 ± 0.2, n = 9 cells; indirect IPSCs, 11.8 ± 2.3, n = 19 cells from 9 mice, Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by latency measurements from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The faster onset latencies of direct IPSCs compared to nEPSCs and indirect IPSCs are consistent with monosynaptic release of GABA by cholinergic neurons.
source: These data suggest direct IPSCs are independent of nAChR signaling and mediated by GABAA receptors, consistent with monosynaptic release of GABA by cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of fast onset latencies, pharmacological independence from nAChR signaling, and GABAA receptor mediation.

claim: In cortex, GP, NB, and MS/DBB, nearly all ChAT+ cells were Slc32a1+ (zsGreen+/ChAT+, from 3 mice: Ctx, 628/628; GP, 238/243; NB, 598/624; MS/DBB; 560/601).
source: In cortex, GP, NB, and MS/DBB, nearly all of ChAT+ cell were Slc32a1+ (zsGreen+/ChAT+, from 3 mice: Ctx, 628/628; GP, 238/243; NB, 598/624; MS/DBB; 560/601, Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of colocalization between zsGreen Cre reporter and ChAT immunostaining shown in Figure 2.

claim: ChAT+ cells of the PPN very rarely expressed Slc32a1 (3/157).
source: In contrast, ChAT+ cells of the PPN very rarely expressed Slc32a1 (3/157, Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of colocalization in PPN shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In both cortical and subcortical forebrain regions, ChAT+ cells express the canonical molecular machinery to package GABA into vesicles.
source: These data suggest that in both cortical and subcortical forebrain regions, ChAT+ cells express the canonical molecular machinery to package GABA into vesicles.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ChAT+ cells in these regions express Slc32a1, the vesicular GABA transporter.

claim: GABAergic marker Slc32a1 is not a ubiquitous feature of the central cholinergic system, as ChAT+ neurons in the brainstem PPN do not express Slc32a1.
source: However, since ChAT+ neurons in the brainstem PPN do not express Slc32a1, this GABAergic marker is not a ubiquitous feature of the central cholinergic system.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PPN ChAT+ neurons lack Slc32a1 expression while other forebrain cholinergic populations express it.

claim: GAD67 is expressed largely in cell bodies and is thought to be responsible for synthesizing GABA for general metabolic cell functions.
source: GAD67 is expressed largely in cell bodies and is thought to be responsible for synthesizing GABA for general metabolic cell functions, whereas GAD65 expression is more prominent in axon terminals and is thought to mediate the majority of synthesis of synaptic GABA (Soghomonian and Martin, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on GAD67 function and localization.

claim: GAD65 expression is more prominent in axon terminals and is thought to mediate the majority of synthesis of synaptic GABA.
source: GAD67 is expressed largely in cell bodies and is thought to be responsible for synthesizing GABA for general metabolic cell functions, whereas GAD65 expression is more prominent in axon terminals and is thought to mediate the majority of synthesis of synaptic GABA (Soghomonian and Martin, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on GAD65 function and localization.

claim: Only minor overlap was detected between neurons that stained positive for ChAT and those that expressed GFP (Gad1) in the NB, GP, MS/DBB, or PPN (GFP+/ChAT + neurons: MS/DBB, 1/573; NB, 0/439; GP, 7/413; PPN, 12/246).
source: We detected only minor overlap between neurons that stained positive for ChAT and those that expressed GFP in the NB, GP, MS/DBB, or PPN, except for cortical ChAT+ interneurons, where we observed significant overlap (GFP+/ChAT + neurons: Ctx: 122/136; MS/DBB, 1/573; NB, 0/439; GP, 7/413; PPN, 12/246, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of colocalization between GFP and ChAT in Gad1GFP mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant overlap was observed between neurons that stained positive for ChAT and those that expressed GFP (Gad1) in cortical ChAT+ interneurons (122/136).
source: We detected only minor overlap between neurons that stained positive for ChAT and those that expressed GFP in the NB, GP, MS/DBB, or PPN, except for cortical ChAT+ interneurons, where we observed significant overlap (GFP+/ChAT + neurons: Ctx: 122/136; MS/DBB, 1/573; NB, 0/439; GP, 7/413; PPN, 12/246, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of colocalization in cortex shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Within the major subcortical cholinergic projections, GAD67-mediated GABA synthesis does not occur in cholinergic neurons.
source: This suggests that within the major subcortical cholinergic projections, GAD67-mediated GABA synthesis does not occur in cholinergic neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of Gad1/ChAT colocalization in subcortical cholinergic regions.

claim: In cortex, GP, NB, and MS/DBB of Gad2 i-Cre; Rosa26 lsl-zsGreen mice, most ChAT+ neurons were Gad2+ (zsGreen+/ChAT+, from 4 mice: Ctx, 518/519; GP, 273/372; NB, 860/934; MS/DBB, 673/685).
source: In contrast to Gad1, in cortex, GP, NB, and MS/DBB of Gad2 i-Cre; Rosa26 lsl-zsGreen mice, most ChAT+ neurons were Gad2+ (zsGreen+/ChAT+, from 4 mice: Ctx, 518/519; GP, 273/372; NB, 860/934; MS/DBB, 673/685, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of colocalization between zsGreen Cre reporter and ChAT immunostaining in Gad2 i-Cre mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the brainstem PPN, few of the ChAT+ cells were Gad2+ (6/110).
source: In the brainstem, however, few of the ChAT+ cells were Gad2+ (PPN, 6/110, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of colocalization in PPN shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ChAT co-expression pattern for Gad2 is similar to Slc32a1, suggesting that forebrain cholinergic neurons possess the necessary cellular machinery to both synthesize and package synaptic GABA.
source: This ChAT co-expression pattern for Gad2 is similar to Slc32a1, suggesting that forebrain cholinergic neurons possess the necessary cellular machinery to both synthesize and package synaptic GABA.
evidence: Inferred from the similar colocalization patterns of Gad2 and Slc32a1 with ChAT in forebrain regions.

claim: Fast onset IPSCs were observed in 31% of layer 1 interneurons recorded in Chat i-Cre; Slc32a1+/+ mice (n = 5 of 16 from 2 mice).
source: In voltage-clamp recordings from layer 1 interneurons, we observed fast onset IPSCs in 31% of cells recorded in Chat i-Cre; Slc32a1+/+ mice (n = 5 of 16 from 2 mice), but no direct IPSCs in Chat i-Cre; Slc32a1fl/fl mice (n = 0 of 34 cells from 4 mice, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from wild-type mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: No direct IPSCs were observed in Chat i-Cre; Slc32a1fl/fl mice (n = 0 of 34 cells from 4 mice).
source: In voltage-clamp recordings from layer 1 interneurons, we observed fast onset IPSCs in 31% of cells recorded in Chat i-Cre; Slc32a1+/+ mice (n = 5 of 16 from 2 mice), but no direct IPSCs in Chat i-Cre; Slc32a1fl/fl mice (n = 0 of 34 cells from 4 mice, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from Slc32a1 conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proportion and average peak amplitude of nAChR responses remains unchanged between Slc32a1+/+ and Slc32a1fl/fl mice.
source: In contrast, the proportion and average peak amplitude of nAChR responses remains unchanged between Slc32a1+/+ and Slc32a1fl/fl mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of nEPSC amplitudes between genotypes shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GABA release from cholinergic neurons relies on cell autonomous Slc32a1, ruling out a disynaptic mechanism.
source: These data demonstrate that GABA but not ACh release from cholinergic neurons relies on cell autonomous Slc32a1, ruling out a disynaptic mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the selective elimination of IPSCs but not nEPSCs in Slc32a1 conditional knockout mice.

claim: ACh release from cholinergic neurons does not rely on cell autonomous Slc32a1.
source: These data demonstrate that GABA but not ACh release from cholinergic neurons relies on cell autonomous Slc32a1, ruling out a disynaptic mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of nEPSCs in Slc32a1 conditional knockout mice.

claim: Cholinergic neurons release GABA directly.
source: Indeed, conditional knock-out of Slc32a1 selectively in cholinergic neurons eliminates light-evoked monosynaptic IPSCs. These genetic results confirm that cholinergic neurons release GABA directly.
evidence: Supported by conditional knockout experiments showing elimination of IPSCs when Slc32a1 is deleted from cholinergic neurons.

claim: Cholinergic GABA release is likely to be a feature of most, but not all, central cholinergic neurons.
source: Cholinergic GABA release is likely to be a feature of most, but not all, central cholinergic neurons: the ChAT+ neurons of the MS and DBB—which innervate the hippocampus—also express Gad2 and Slc32a1, whereas those of the midbrain PPN do not.
evidence: Inferred from the differential expression patterns of Gad2 and Slc32a1 across cholinergic populations.

claim: ChAT+ neurons of the MS and DBB express Gad2 and Slc32a1.
source: Cholinergic GABA release is likely to be a feature of most, but not all, central cholinergic neurons: the ChAT+ neurons of the MS and DBB—which innervate the hippocampus—also express Gad2 and Slc32a1, whereas those of the midbrain PPN do not.
evidence: Supported by colocalization data showing Gad2 and Slc32a1 expression in MS/DBB ChAT+ neurons.

claim: ChAT+ neurons of the midbrain PPN do not express Gad2 and Slc32a1.
source: Cholinergic GABA release is likely to be a feature of most, but not all, central cholinergic neurons: the ChAT+ neurons of the MS and DBB—which innervate the hippocampus—also express Gad2 and Slc32a1, whereas those of the midbrain PPN do not.
evidence: Supported by colocalization data showing lack of Gad2 and Slc32a1 expression in PPN ChAT+ neurons.

claim: In retinal SACs, release of GABA and ACh can be functionally separated through patterned light stimulation or pharmacology.
source: In retinal SACs, release of GABA and ACh can be functionally separated through patterned light stimulation or pharmacology.
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings in retinal starburst amacrine cells, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: In Chat+ GP axons in cortex, GABA and ACh appear to be released from distinct vesicular pools which can be located within the same or neighboring pre-synaptic terminals.
source: In Chat+ GP axons in cortex, GABA and ACh appear to be released from distinct vesicular pools which can be located within the same or neighboring pre-synaptic terminals (Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on GP cholinergic neurons.

claim: The differences in the proportion of layer 1 interneurons showing ACh and GABA responses suggest some form of segregated release.
source: Though the precise mechanism by which each forebrain cholinergic population coreleases GABA and ACh remain unclear and further experiments are merited to explore how GABA/ACh cotransmission is regulated, the differences in the proportion of layer 1 interneurons showing ACh and GABA responses suggest some form of segregated release.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different proportions of cells show ACh vs GABA responses.

claim: Anatomical evidence shows widespread distribution of cholinergic fibers through all cortical layers with significant separation between the sites of release and ACh receptors.
source: This model is supported by anatomical evidence showing widespread distribution of cholinergic fibers through all cortical layers with significant separation between the sites of release and ACh receptors (Descarries and Mechawar, 2000; Mechawar et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Behaviorally relevant sensory cues can cause a fast, time-locked spike in ACh concentration, suggesting that ACh may mediate detection of that cue.
source: Behaviorally relevant sensory cues can cause a fast, time-locked spike in ACh concentration, suggesting that ACh may mediate detection of that cue (Parikh et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior behavioral and neurochemical studies.

claim: Fast onset currents mediated by nAChRs can be recorded in cortical interneurons following optogenetic activation of cholinergic fibers.
source: In addition, fast onset currents mediated by nAChRs can be recorded in cortical interneurons following optogenetic activation of cholinergic fibers (Arroyo et al., 2012; Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior optogenetic studies.

claim: The finding that cholinergic neurons elicit fast-onset synaptic GABAA responses lends further support to the notion that the cholinergic system can rapidly affect cortical computations by acting at classical synapses.
source: Our finding that cholinergic neurons also elicit fast-onset synaptic GABAA responses lends further support to the notion that the cholinergic system can rapidly affect cortical computations by acting at classical synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of fast GABA responses observed in this study and prior evidence of fast cholinergic signaling.

claim: ACh release from basal forebrain neurons excites layer 1 and VIP+ interneurons, which in turn inhibit local interneurons that target principle neurons of the cortex.
source: ACh release from basal forebrain neurons excites layer 1 and VIP+ interneurons, which in turn inhibit local interneurons that target principle neurons of the cortex (Letzkus et al., 2011; Pinto et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on cholinergic disinhibition.

claim: Depending on the timing and targeted cell types, GABA corelease could conceivably enhance the disinhibitory effect by inhibiting local interneurons, thereby promoting cortical activity.
source: Depending on the timing and targeted cell types, GABA corelease could conceivably enhance this effect by inhibiting local interneurons, thereby promoting cortical activity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential circuit-level effects of GABA corelease.

claim: In hippocampal interneurons, post-synaptic nAChRs are present in inhibitory synapses.
source: For example, in hippocampal interneurons, post-synaptic nAChRs are present in inhibitory synapses (Fabian-Fine et al., 2001) and when activated, reduce GABAA receptor-mediated IPSCs in a Ca2+ and PKC-dependent manner (Wanaverbecq et al., 2007; Zhang and Berg, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior anatomical study.

claim: When activated, post-synaptic nAChRs in hippocampal interneurons reduce GABAA receptor-mediated IPSCs in a Ca2+ and PKC-dependent manner.
source: For example, in hippocampal interneurons, post-synaptic nAChRs are present in inhibitory synapses (Fabian-Fine et al., 2001) and when activated, reduce GABAA receptor-mediated IPSCs in a Ca2+ and PKC-dependent manner (Wanaverbecq et al., 2007; Zhang and Berg, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: Coreleased ACh and GABA could interact to modulate local synaptic signaling.
source: Thus coreleased ACh and GABA could interact to modulate local synaptic signaling.
evidence: Inferred from prior evidence of nAChR modulation of GABA signaling and the finding of ACh/GABA corelease.

claim: Activity within the basal forebrain cholinergic projection is necessary and sufficient for plasticity in sensory cortices.
source: Lastly, experiments poisoning or stimulating the basal forebrain cholinergic system have demonstrated that activity within this projection is necessary and sufficient for plasticity in sensory cortices (Kilgard and Merzenich, 1998; Weinberger, 2004; Ramanathan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies on cholinergic system and plasticity.

claim: ACh alone can induce functional changes in cortical circuits.
source: While ACh alone can induce functional changes in cortical circuits (Metherate and Weinberger, 1990), GABA may also contribute to synaptic rewiring in vivo.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on ACh-induced plasticity.

claim: GABA may contribute to synaptic rewiring in vivo.
source: While ACh alone can induce functional changes in cortical circuits (Metherate and Weinberger, 1990), GABA may also contribute to synaptic rewiring in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential role of GABA in plasticity.

claim: Given the presence of GABA signaling machinery throughout the distinct forebrain cholinergic systems, corelease likely has a significant and fundamental effect on brain activity and cognition.
source: Given the presence of GABA signaling machinery throughout the distinct forebrain cholinergic systems, corelease likely has a significant and fundamental effect on brain activity and cognition.
evidence: Inferred from the widespread expression of GABA machinery in forebrain cholinergic neurons and speculative reasoning about functional implications.

claim: Neurotransmitter corelease is emerging as a common theme of central neuromodulatory systems.
source: Neurotransmitter corelease is emerging as a common theme of central neuromodulatory systems.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Corelease of glutamate or GABA with acetylcholine has been reported within the cholinergic system.
source: Though corelease of glutamate or GABA with acetylcholine has been reported within the cholinergic system, the full extent is unknown.
evidence: This statement references prior reports in the literature, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Retinal starburst amacrine cells (SACs) differentially release GABA and acetylcholine (ACh) based on the pattern of light stimulation.
source: Retinal starburst amacrine cells (SACs) differentially release GABA and acetylcholine (ACh) based on the pattern of light stimulation (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on retinal SACs.

claim: Selective activation of striatal cholinergic interneurons results in cholinergic and glutamatergic responses.
source: In the central brain, selective activation of striatal cholinergic interneurons results in cholinergic and glutamatergic responses (Gras et al., 2008; Higley et al., 2011; Nelson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on striatal cholinergic neurons.

claim: The cholinergic projection from habenula excites interpeduncular neurons through glutamate and ACh.
source: Similarly, the cholinergic projection from habenula excites interpeduncular neurons through glutamate and ACh (Ren et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on habenula cholinergic neurons.

claim: The dorsal-most BFC neurons, which belong to the globus pallidus externus (GP), express molecular markers for GABA synthesis and vesicular packaging.
source: The dorsal-most BFC neurons, which belong to the globus pallidus externus (GP), express molecular markers for GABA synthesis and vesicular packaging and trigger GABAA receptor currents in GP and cortex when activated (Tkatch et al., 1998; Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on GP cholinergic neurons.

claim: The dorsal-most BFC neurons trigger GABAA receptor currents in GP and cortex when activated.
source: The dorsal-most BFC neurons, which belong to the globus pallidus externus (GP), express molecular markers for GABA synthesis and vesicular packaging and trigger GABAA receptor currents in GP and cortex when activated (Tkatch et al., 1998; Saunders et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on GP cholinergic neurons.

claim: Stimulation of dopaminergic terminals from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra compacta activates glutamate-mediated excitatory currents in the nucleus accumbens.
source: In addition to the impact of dopamine, stimulation of dopaminergic terminals from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra compacta activates glutamate-mediated excitatory currents in the nucleus accumbens (Stuber et al., 2010; Tecuapetla et al., 2010) and GABA-mediated inhibitory currents in the striatum (Tritsch et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on dopaminergic neuron corelease.

claim: Stimulation of dopaminergic terminals from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra compacta activates GABA-mediated inhibitory currents in the striatum.
source: In addition to the impact of dopamine, stimulation of dopaminergic terminals from the ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra compacta activates glutamate-mediated excitatory currents in the nucleus accumbens (Stuber et al., 2010; Tecuapetla et al., 2010) and GABA-mediated inhibitory currents in the striatum (Tritsch et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on dopaminergic neuron corelease.

claim: Serotonergic neurons of the dorsal raphe can trigger glutamate-mediated currents in post-synaptic neurons of the ventral tegmentum and nucleus accumbens which contributes to the signaling of reward.
source: Likewise, serotonergic neurons of the dorsal raphe can trigger glutamate-mediated currents in post-synaptic neurons of the ventral tegmentum and nucleus accumbens which contributes to the signaling of reward (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on serotonergic neuron corelease.

claim: In dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra, GABA is co-packaged with dopamine into vesicles by the transporter VMAT2 (Slc18a2).
source: In those neurons, GABA is co-packaged with dopamine into vesicles by the transporter VMAT2 (Slc18a2), instead of by the typical vesicular transporter for GABA (VGAT, encoded by Slc32a1), which is necessary for packaging in most GABAergic neurons (Wojcik et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2008; Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on GABA packaging in dopaminergic neurons.

claim: VGAT (encoded by Slc32a1) is necessary for GABA packaging in most GABAergic neurons.
source: In those neurons, GABA is co-packaged with dopamine into vesicles by the transporter VMAT2 (Slc18a2), instead of by the typical vesicular transporter for GABA (VGAT, encoded by Slc32a1), which is necessary for packaging in most GABAergic neurons (Wojcik et al., 2006; Tong et al., 2008; Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on VGAT function.

claim: Both GABA and glycine packaging in spinal interneurons rely on VGAT.
source: Similarly, both GABA and glycine packaging in spinal interneurons rely on VGAT (Wojcik et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study on spinal interneuron neurotransmitter packaging.

claim: Coreleased GABA and glutamate are thought to control the balance of excitation and inhibition in the lateral habenula.
source: In other instances, the effects of the two neurotransmitters may be different and synergistic. For example, coreleased GABA and glutamate are thought to control the balance of excitation and inhibition in the lateral habenula (Root et al., 2014; Shabel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on lateral habenula neurotransmission.

claim: In GABA/glutamate corelease onto neurons of the lateral habenula, individual miniature EPSCs can be observed with dual GABA/glutamate components.
source: This is the case for GABA/glutamate corelease onto neurons of the lateral habenula, where individual miniature EPSCs can be observed with dual GABA/glutamate components (Shabel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study demonstrating co-packaging of GABA and glutamate.
